title: Geometry Part 1: Lines, Angles, Triangles, Area and Volume
lead: Geometry and Trigonometry is about 15% of the Math section, roughly 5 to 7 of the 44 questions, so it gets two classes. This one covers the reference sheet, angle rules, triangles and similarity, quadrilaterals, figures on the coordinate plane, and area and volume. Right triangles, trigonometry and circles come in Class 24. There are no proofs on the SAT. You apply a small set of rules to find an angle, a length, an area or a volume, and the hard questions mix geometry with algebra.

parts.title: Part 1 · The reference sheet
parts.html:
The reference sheet opens from the button at the top right of the Bluebook screen. It gives you:

The reference sheet in Bluebook gives you:

  • Area and circumference: circle, rectangle, triangle.
  • Pythagorean theorem: a² + b² = c².
  • Special right triangles: the 30-60-90 and 45-45-90 side ratios.
  • Volume: rectangular prism, cylinder, sphere, cone, pyramid.
  • Facts: a circle has 360° or 2π radians; the angles of a triangle add to 180°.

What it does not give you. These must be known by heart.

  • Slope, and the slope-intercept form of a line (Class 5).
  • The distance and midpoint formulas (Part 6 below).
  • The area of a trapezoid (Part 5 below).
  • Arc length and sector area (Class 24).
  • Every angle rule in Part 2.

Tip. Do not compute an area or volume from memory. Take the formula from the reference sheet, so you never mix up 2πr (circumference) and πr² (area).

parts.title: Part 2 · Lines and angles
parts.html:
Angle questions look crowded, but they come down to a few rules. Learn the vocabulary first, because the question will use it.

TermMeaning
Complementary anglesTwo angles that add to 90°.
Supplementary anglesTwo angles that add to 180°.
Adjacent anglesTwo angles that share a vertex and one side.
Linear pairTwo adjacent angles that form a straight line. They add to 180°.
Vertical anglesThe opposite angles where two lines cross. They are equal.
Angles around a pointThey add to 360°.
TransversalA line that crosses two other lines.

Parallel lines and a transversal. In the figure, lines ℓ and m are parallel.

PairIn the figureRule
Vertical angles1 and 4, 2 and 3, 5 and 8, 6 and 7Equal
Corresponding angles (same position at each crossing)1 and 5, 2 and 6, 3 and 7, 4 and 8Equal
Alternate interior angles (between the lines, opposite sides)3 and 6, 4 and 5Equal
Same-side interior angles (between the lines, same side)3 and 5, 4 and 6Add to 180°

With two parallel lines and a transversal there are only two angle sizes. All the acute angles are equal, all the obtuse angles are equal, and one of each adds to 180°.

In the figure, angle 2 measures 118°. What is the measure of angle 5? Angle 6 corresponds to angle 2 → 118°
Angles 5 and 6 are a linear pair → 180°−118°=62°

Two more rules

  • Exterior angle of a triangle: it equals the sum of the two interior angles that are not next to it.
  • Polygon angle sum: the interior angles of an n-sided polygon add to (n − 2) × 180°.
Polygon angle sums Triangle: (3−2)×180°=180°
Quadrilateral: (4−2)×180°=360°
Hexagon: (6−2)×180°=720°, so each angle of a regular hexagon is 720°6=120°

Tip. Start every angle question by marking the parallel lines, right angles and crossing lines on your sketch. Then look for a pair from the tables above that you can use straight away.

parts.title: Part 3 · Triangle facts
parts.html:
TriangleWhat you know
Any triangleThe three angles add to 180°.
IsoscelesTwo equal sides, and the angles opposite those sides are equal.
EquilateralThree equal sides and three 60° angles.
RightOne 90° angle. The Pythagorean theorem applies to right triangles only (Class 24).
In an isosceles triangle, the angle between the two equal sides measures 40°. What is the measure of each of the other angles? The other two angles are equal: 40+2x=180
2x=140 → x=70 → 70° each

parts.title: Part 4 · Similar triangles
parts.html:
Similar triangles have the same angles, even at different sizes, so their side lengths are proportional.

  • If triangle A has sides 3, 4, 5 and triangle B is similar with a scale factor of 2, its sides are 6, 8, 10.
  • Areas scale by the square of the factor: triangle B has 2² = 4 times the area of triangle A.
  • The SAT trick: similar triangles are hidden by nesting, a small triangle inside a larger one. Redraw them as two separate triangles to see the ratios.

Where similarity appears

  • A segment is drawn inside a triangle parallel to one side. The small triangle it cuts off is similar to the whole triangle.
  • Two triangles share an angle and have a second pair of equal angles (often two right angles, or vertical angles).

Two matching angles are enough. The third pair must match because every triangle adds to 180°.

Example. In triangle ABC, point D is on side AB and point E is on side AC, with DE parallel to BC. AD=6, DB=3 and DE=8. What is the length of BC? Triangle ADE is similar to triangle ABC
Whole side: AB=6+3=9
ADAB=DEBC → 69=8BC
6×BC=72 → BC=12

Common mistake. Using a piece of a side where the whole side belongs. The ratio 6/3 compares AD with DB, and DB is not a side of either triangle. Match small-triangle side to big-triangle side: AD with AB, DE with BC.

Once the triangles are identified, the rest is the proportion work from Class 15.

parts.title: Part 5 · Quadrilaterals, area and scaling
parts.html:
ShapePropertiesArea
RectangleFour 90° angles; opposite sides equallength × width
SquareFour 90° angles; all sides equalside²
ParallelogramOpposite sides parallel and equal; opposite angles equalbase × height
TrapezoidOne pair of parallel sides½ × (base 1 + base 2) × height
Triangle½ × base × height
Circleπr²

The height is always measured at a right angle to the base. In a parallelogram or trapezoid it is not the slanted side.

A trapezoid has parallel sides of 7 and 13 and a height of 6. What is its area? 12×(7+13)×6=12×20×6=60

Before you substitute. The SAT tests whether you can apply a formula to a situation, and most errors come from substituting too early.

  • What is being asked? Area or perimeter? Surface area or volume? Fencing a garden is perimeter; covering it with soil is area.
  • Which units? Lengths are in units, areas in square units, volumes in cubic units. If the units in the answer choices do not match your result, you computed the wrong quantity.
  • Is there scaling language? “Doubled”, “three times as long”, “a scale model” all point to the rule below.

Scaling. When every length of a shape is multiplied by k, the perimeter is multiplied by k, the area by k², and the volume by k³.

A square has side 5. Each side is tripled. What happens to the area? Scale factor 3 → area ×32=9
Check: 52=25 and 152=225=9×25

parts.title: Part 6 · Figures on the coordinate plane
parts.html:
When a figure is drawn on a grid, geometry becomes algebra. Slope, parallel lines (equal slopes) and perpendicular lines (slopes that multiply to −1) are in Class 5. Two more tools are needed here, and neither is on the reference sheet.

ToolFormulaWhat it is
Distance√[(x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²]The Pythagorean theorem, with the horizontal and vertical changes as the legs
Midpoint((x₁ + x₂) / 2, (y₁ + y₂) / 2)The average of the x-values and the average of the y-values
Find the length and the midpoint of the segment from (1,2) to (7,10). Horizontal change 6, vertical change 8
Length: 62+82=100=10
Midpoint: (1+72,2+102)=(4,6)

If you forget the distance formula, draw the right triangle under the segment and use the Pythagorean theorem. It is the same calculation.

Choosing the tool. A figure on a grid looks like geometry and behaves like algebra.

The question is about…Use
Direction: are two sides parallel or perpendicular?Slope
Length: how long is a side, or are two sides equal?Distance
Halfway: the center of a segment, or a line that bisects itMidpoint
  1. Copy the coordinates and label the points.
  2. Decide what is being tested: direction, length or halfway.
  3. Use that one tool and simplify.
The vertices of a quadrilateral are A(0,0), B(4,2), C(5,6) and D(1,4). Is side AB parallel to side DC? Direction → slope
AB: 2−04−0=12
DC: 6−45−1=12
Equal slopes → parallel

parts.title: Part 7 · Volume
parts.html:
Three-dimensional shapes are not frequent, and the questions are usually direct. All five formulas are on the reference sheet.

SolidVolume
Rectangular prismlength × width × height
Cylinderπr²h
Sphere(4/3)πr³
Cone(1/3)πr²h
Pyramid with a rectangular base(1/3) × length × width × height

A prism or cylinder is base area × height. A cone or pyramid is one third of that.

A cylinder has a diameter of 6 and a height of 10. What is its volume? Radius =6÷2=3
π×32×10=90π

Check whether the question gives the radius or the diameter. Using 6 as the radius gives 360π, which will be among the choices.

The trap is units. The question gives the radius in inches and asks for the volume in cubic feet. Convert the lengths before you plug them into the formula. Converting a radius is one step. Converting a finished volume means using the conversion factor three times (1 cubic foot = 12 × 12 × 12 cubic inches).

parts.title: Part 8 · Working with diagrams
parts.html:
When a geometry question will not start, the problem is usually how the diagram is being read, not a missing formula.

Use only what is stated or marked. A figure is a list of facts, not a picture. Many figures are drawn accurately, and some carry the note “Figure not drawn to scale”. In both cases, how a figure looks is not something you may use.

FactIt counts only if…
Equal lengthsthe sides have matching tick marks, or the text says so
Equal anglesthe angles have matching arcs, or the text says so
Parallel linesthe lines have matching arrows, or the text says so
A right anglethere is a small square in the corner, or the text says so

Common trap. A triangle looks isosceles, or an angle looks like 90°. If it is not marked or stated, do not use it.

Mark the figure before solving. Each mark tells you which rule to look for.

You are toldLook for
Parallel linesCorresponding and alternate interior angles
Perpendicular linesComplementary angles and right triangles
Equal sidesAn isosceles triangle, so equal angles
Equal anglesSimilar triangles
A midpoint or a bisectorTwo equal parts, or proportional segments

No figure given? Translate in three steps.

  1. Words → sketch. Draw the simplest version of the situation. It does not need to be neat.
  2. Sketch → labels. Write every given value on it, with units, and name the unknown.
  3. Labels → equation. Choose the one relationship that fits: an angle sum, a similarity ratio, an area or volume formula, or the distance formula.

Two habits

  • Underline what is asked. Radius or diameter? Area or perimeter? One side or the whole length?
  • Turn comparisons into expressions first. “Twice as long as the width” is 2w. “5 more than the width” is w + 5. “Increased by 20%” is 1.2 times the original. Write these before substituting anything.
A rectangle's length is 3 more than twice its width. Its perimeter is 36. What is its area? Sketch a rectangle: width w, length 2w+3
Perimeter: 2(w+2w+3)=36 → 6w+6=36 → w=5
Length: 2(5)+3=13
Asked for area: 5×13=65

The choices will include 5 and 13. Both are steps on the way, not the answer.

parts.title: Part 9 · Congruence, density and unequal scaling
parts.html:
Congruent triangles have the same shape and the same size: all three pairs of sides and all three pairs of angles match. Four sets of information are enough to prove it.

RuleWhat must match
SSSAll three pairs of sides
SASTwo pairs of sides and the angle between them
ASATwo pairs of angles and the side between them
AASTwo pairs of angles and a side not between them

Two sides and an angle that is not between them (SSA) is not enough. For similarity, two pairs of equal angles are enough.

The order of the letters tells you what matches. If triangle ABC is congruent or similar to triangle DEF, then A matches D, B matches E and C matches F, so side AB matches DE and side AC matches DF. You can set up the proportion from the names alone, without a figure.

Triangles ABC and DEF are congruent, with A matching D. Angles B and E each measure 50°, and angle C measures 25°. What is the measure of angle D? Angle F matches angle C → 25°
Angle D=180°−50°−25°=105°

Density = mass ÷ volume. It is not on the reference sheet.

A block has a volume of 2.5 cubic metres and a mass of 2,000 kilograms. What is its density? 2000÷2.5=800 kilograms per cubic metre

When the dimensions change by different factors, the k² and k³ rules from Part 5 do not apply. Put each factor into the formula where its dimension appears.

The radius of a cylinder is doubled and its height is halved. What happens to the volume? Volume =πr2h → the radius factor is squared, the height factor is not
22×12=2 → the volume doubles
